idiom_name: JVM interning plus scala.collection.mutable.WeakHashMap or TrieMap pool
implementation_notes: On the JVM the factory already exists for common cases: String.intern() returns the canonical string, the boxed-primitive caches behind Integer.valueOf are mandated, and case classes plus enum values give canonical instances cheaply. For custom intrinsic state the standard library offers scala.collection.mutable.WeakHashMap, which wraps java.util.WeakHashMap so entries disappear when no context strongly references the key, and scala.collection.concurrent.TrieMap for lock-free concurrent creation; a plain HashMap with a synchronized guard is the simplest form. The roles stay explicit: an immutable case class for the shared state and a separate case class or tuple holding the extrinsic fields plus the reference.
code_sketch:
case class Glyph(code: String, w: Int, h: Int)     // intrinsic, immutable

object GlyphFactory {                              // FlyweightFactory
  private val pool = scala.collection.mutable.WeakHashMap.empty[String, Glyph]
  def apply(code: String, w: Int, h: Int): Glyph =
    pool.synchronized(pool.getOrElseUpdate(code, Glyph(code, w, h)))
}

case class Cell(glyph: Glyph, x: Int, y: Int)      // extrinsic state
pitfalls: WeakHashMap entries vanish as soon as the key is only weakly reachable, so a client re-looking-up by an equal but distinct key can get a second instance; use a strong map when identity must be stable.
case class copy() is shallow and case classes are only as immutable as their fields: an Array or mutable collection inside a shared Glyph leaks mutation to every context.
String.intern() pins strings in the JVM's native intern table shared with the entire process, including libraries; restrict it to a small bounded vocabulary.
pool.synchronized serializes every lookup on the whole map, which becomes a bottleneck in hot interning paths; TrieMap or a pre-filled immutable map is better for read-mostly workloads.
